title: Just one thing
hookLine: abandon greed, just that one thing, and I guarantee the fruit
carry: pull it up by the root
last: SHE CAME BACK WITH SOMETHING BETTER.

lines: A LIST CAN BE A DELAY.
cards: Self-help shelves are full of lists. Seven habits. Twelve rules.
Thirty days to a better you. Lists are useful, and Buddhist texts love them too: four truths, eight factors, five hindrances.
But sometimes a list is a way of putting things off; there's always one more item to read about before starting. The Itivuttaka opens with no list at all.
Its section of ones begins with a single thing, and an unusual promise. The Buddha doesn't say try this. He says: I guarantee it.

teach.b: Here is the first teaching of the book, after the opening line. Abandon one thing, monks, and I am your guarantee of non-return. What one thing?

Non-return is a technical term: in the early texts, the third of four stages of awakening, someone who won't be reborn in this world of the senses again. So the promise is enormous, and the condition is one thing.
The verse explains: driven by greed, beings go to a bad destination; seeing greed rightly, those who understand let it go, and having let it go, they don't come back to this world.
Then the very next teachings say the same, one at a time. Abandon one thing: hatred. Then delusion.
Then anger, then contempt, then conceit.
Each one alone, with the same guarantee. Why would one be enough? The text doesn't say.
One way teachers explain it: these aren't six separate weeds; pull one up by the root, really by the root, and the others turn out to grow from the same soil.
And the word guarantee: the Pali, patibhoga, means a guarantor, someone who stands surety. In the text, the Buddha puts his own word behind the promise.

how: Buddhist teachers often name greed, hatred and delusion as the three roots of unwholesome action, and some practitioners work with one of them at a time.

games.q: just one thing: tap the pairs.

s: the Itivuttaka opens with a long list of rules
it opens with one thing: abandon greed.
the Buddha says 'I am your guarantee' of non-return
he puts himself on the line for the one who lets go of greed.
the same promise is made for hatred and delusion, one at a time
the next teachings repeat it for hatred, delusion, anger, contempt and conceit.

games.q: you want to make real progress on the path. the Itivuttaka's first teaching offers a deal. what is it?
o: master eight things and you might succeed.
abandon just greed, and the Buddha guarantees non-return.
games.why: one thing, and a guarantee. the same offer follows for hatred, delusion, anger, contempt and conceit.

practice: Ask where a little greed shows up in your day: a second helping you don't want, checking a price again, wanting the last word.
Choose just one small one, picture the moment it usually happens, and picture yourself letting it go, hand open, breath out.

wordCard.voice: Lobha, greed. The opening of the Itivuttaka: abandon this, just that, and the Buddha stands as your guarantee. Today's word.

orig.note: Pali lobha: greed, the one thing to abandon in Itivuttaka 1, first of the three unwholesome roots.

carryVoice: Your line: pull it up by the root. One thing, with the Buddha's own word behind it. Six hundred twenty-seven days now.

sources.ref: Itivuttaka 1–6 (Lobha, Dosa, Moha, Kodha, Makkha, Mana Suttas)
